viscous

VIS-kus -- from Latin viscosus, 'sticky,' from viscum, 'mistletoe' -- ancient birdlime, a sticky trap for birds, was made from mistletoe berries. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Viscous is thick, sticky, and syrupy.

The paint had gone viscous after sitting open for a week, forming thick clumps that clogged the brush.

Worked Example

Left in the freezer overnight, the honey turned so slow and heavy that it barely dripped off the spoon even after a full minute of waiting.

Viscous describes a liquid thick and sticky enough to resist flowing easily -- honey that barely drips even after a full minute is a textbook example of viscosity at work.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sticky: Sticky describes how a surface grips -- tape, sap, and jam hold on to whatever touches them. Viscous describes how a liquid flows: slowly, heavily, resisting the pour. The two often travel together, but they are separate properties: cold gravy is viscous without gripping anything at all.

gooey: Gooey is the casual, kid-friendly word for something soft, thick, and sticky at once -- melted marshmallow, the middle of a warm brownie. Viscous is the precise, almost scientific term for a liquid that resists flowing. A lab report calls a sample viscous; nobody's chemistry teacher writes gooey.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

watery: thin and easily poured, like water

runny: flowing easily, without resistance

Where it sits · how slowly it pours and clings — thick → viscous → syrupy

thick vs. viscous: Thick is the everyday word for any dense consistency, solid or liquid, while viscous is a more precise, almost scientific term specifically about how a liquid flows.

syrupy vs. viscous: Syrupy pushes the image further than viscous, calling up the exact slow-pouring, sticky feel of actual syrup or honey.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — visc-

root — visc-: sticky substance, mistletoe/birdlime (Latin viscum)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Viscous comes from Latin viscosus, 'sticky,' from viscum, the Latin word for both mistletoe and the sticky birdlime once made from its berries to trap small birds -- something viscous is, at its root, as sticky as ancient birdlime.

Use the root in a new word: viscosity

Use the root in a new word: viscosity: Scientists measure a liquid's viscosity to predict exactly how slowly it will pour.
